claim: Mubritinib does not inhibit HER2 phosphorylation directly.
source: Surprisingly, there was only a small decrease in HER2 phosphorylation in the presence of mubritinib, in contrast to lapatinib.
evidence: Western blot analysis showing minimal effect on HER2 phosphorylation compared to lapatinib, and radiometric kinase assays showing no decrease in 32P incorporation even at 10 μM mubritinib.

claim: Mubritinib alters the phosphorylation status of proteins downstream of the energy sensor AMPK.
source: In agreement with these data, we show that treatment of cells with mubritinib (Figure 1B) alters the phosphorylation status of proteins downstream of the energy sensor AMPK (e.g. acetyl-CoA carboxylase) and impacts on mTOR signalling (e.g. phosphorylation of RPS6, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blot data showing changes in ACC and RPS6 phosphorylation following mubritinib treatment.

claim: Mubritinib did not decrease 32P incorporation in HER2 kinase assays even at 10 μM.
source: Mubritinib did not decrease 32P incorporation, even at 10 μM (Figure 1C and D), demonstrating that it does not inhibit HER2 phosphorylation.
evidence: Radiometric kinase assay data showing no inhibition of HER2 activity by mubritinib.

claim: Mubritinib displays no activity against almost 300 other kinases screened.
source: Furthermore, consistent with our data (Figure 1E), mubritinib has been reported to display no activity against almost 300 other kinases screened (Anastassiadis et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to published kinase screening data and supporting experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure of H9c2 cells to 2 μM mubritinib for 2 hr in galactose-containing media led to a 50% decrease in ATP levels.
source: Exposure of H9c2 cells to 2 μM mubritinib for 2 hr in galactose-containing media led to a 50% decrease in ATP levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: ATP measurement data from H9c2 cells treated with mubritinib in galactose media.

claim: Prolonged exposure to mubritinib depleted ATP levels to 10% of the control value in H9c2 cells.
source: Furthermore, prolonged exposure depleted ATP levels to 10% of the control value (Figure 1F) and induced cell death (Figure 1G).
evidence: Time course ATP measurement data showing progressive depletion over 24 hours.

claim: Prolonged exposure to mubritinib induced cell death in H9c2 cells.
source: Furthermore, prolonged exposure depleted ATP levels to 10% of the control value (Figure 1F) and induced cell death (Figure 1G).
evidence: Cell viability data using DRAQ7 staining and Annexin-V-FITC labelling showing increased cell death over 72 hours.

claim: Mubritinib inhibits ATP production in hESC-cardiomyocytes in galactose-containing media but not glucose-containing media.
source: Importantly, inhibition of ATP production in galactose (but not glucose) containing media by mubritinib and other inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation was also observed in hESC-CMs (Figure 1H) and had a profound effect on cell beat rate (Figure 1I).
evidence: ATP measurement data from hESC-cardiomyocytes showing differential effects in glucose vs galactose media.

claim: Mubritinib has a profound effect on hESC-cardiomyocyte beat rate.
source: Importantly, inhibition of ATP production in galactose (but not glucose) containing media by mubritinib and other inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation was also observed in hESC-CMs (Figure 1H) and had a profound effect on cell beat rate (Figure 1I).
evidence: Multi-electrode array data showing decreased beat rate in cardiomyocytes treated with mubritinib.

claim: Mubritinib has been shown recently to target respiratory complex I and inhibit growth of cancer cells from patients with AML.
source: It has been shown recently that mubritinib targets respiratory complex I and inhibits growth of cancer cells from patients with AML, which are highly dependent on oxidative phosphorylation for survival (Baccelli et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to published work by Baccelli et al., 2019.

claim: In H9c2 or hESC-CMs cells exposed to mubritinib the rotenone-sensitive OCR decreased by ~50%.
source: However, in H9c2 or hESC-CMs cells exposed to mubritinib the rotenone-sensitive OCR decreased by ~50% (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Seahorse oxygen consumption rate measurements showing approximately 50% reduction in rotenone-sensitive respiration.

claim: Mubritinib inhibits pyruvate/malate-driven respiration in plasma-membrane permeabilised H9c2 cells.
source: All three inhibitors inhibited pyruvate/malate-driven respiration but, crucially, the inhibition of only mubritinib and rotenone was alleviated by subsequent treatment with succinate (Figure 2C), suggesting that mubritinib is a complex I inhibitor.
evidence: Seahorse data from permeabilised cells showing inhibition of complex I-driven respiration that is rescued by succinate.

claim: The inhibition of respiration by mubritinib and rotenone was alleviated by subsequent treatment with succinate.
source: All three inhibitors inhibited pyruvate/malate-driven respiration but, crucially, the inhibition of only mubritinib and rotenone was alleviated by subsequent treatment with succinate (Figure 2C), suggesting that mubritinib is a complex I inhibitor.
evidence: Seahorse data showing restoration of respiration with succinate after mubritinib treatment, indicating complex I-specific inhibition.

claim: Mubritinib showed a dose-dependent decrease in the rate of NADH oxidation in mitochondrial membranes.
source: In agreement with the data obtained from cell lines, mubritinib (1) showed a dose-dependent decrease in the rate of NADH oxidation and no effect on succinate oxidation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Spectrophotometric measurements of NADH oxidation rates at various mubritinib concentrations.

claim: Mubritinib has no effect on succinate oxidation in mitochondrial membranes.
source: In agreement with the data obtained from cell lines, mubritinib (1) showed a dose-dependent decrease in the rate of NADH oxidation and no effect on succinate oxidation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Spectrophotometric measurements showing no change in succinate oxidation rate with mubritinib treatment.

claim: Mubritinib inhibits complex I with an IC50 value of 19.2 nM.
source: The NADH oxidation data were then fit to the standard dose-effect relationship and yielded an IC50 value of 19.2 nM (Figure 2D).
evidence: Dose-response curve fitting of NADH oxidation data from mitochondrial membranes.

claim: APAD+ and FeCN reduction by complex I were unaffected at 500 nM mubritinib.
source: While APAD+ and FeCN reduction were unaffected at 500 nM mubritinib (1), the rate of ubiquinone reduction was essentially abolished (Figure 2E).
evidence: Enzymatic assay data showing no inhibition of artificial electron acceptor reduction.

claim: The rate of ubiquinone reduction by complex I was essentially abolished at 500 nM mubritinib.
source: While APAD+ and FeCN reduction were unaffected at 500 nM mubritinib (1), the rate of ubiquinone reduction was essentially abolished (Figure 2E).
evidence: Enzymatic assay data showing near-complete inhibition of ubiquinone reduction.

claim: Mubritinib inhibits complex I by inhibiting ubiquinone reduction, most likely by binding in the ubiquinone-binding site.
source: These data confirm that mubritinib inhibits complex I directly by inhibiting ubiquinone reduction, most likely by binding in the ubiquinone-binding site.
evidence: Differential inhibition of ubiquinone reduction versus APAD+/FeCN reduction indicates site-specific inhibition.

claim: Compounds 2-4, which have the same N1-linked triazole moiety as mubritinib, retain the ability to inhibit complex I similarly to mubritinib.
source: Compounds 2–4 (Figure 2A), which have the same N1-linked triazole moiety as mubritinib but contain either no substituent (2) or a mild (3) or strong (4) electron donating group in the para-position of the phenyl ring, retain the ability to inhibit complex I, similarly to mubritinib (Figure 2F).
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing similar inhibition by compounds 2-4 compared to mubritinib.

claim: Compound 6, which has the 1,2,3-triazol-1-yl moiety substituted for an isomeric 1,2,3-triazol-2-yl group, is a much weaker inhibitor of complex I.
source: In contrast, compound 6, which has the 1,2,3-triazol-1-yl moiety substituted for an isomeric 1,2,3-triazol-2-yl group, is a much weaker inhibitor (Figure 2F).
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing reduced inhibition by compound 6 compared to mubritinib.

claim: Complete removal of the triazole group in compound 5 resulted in a compound that no longer inhibited NADH oxidation.
source: Complete removal of the triazole group in 5 and modification of the triazole to an N-linked pyrrole in 8, also resulted in compounds that no longer inhibited NADH oxidation (Figure 2F).
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing no inhibition by compound 5.

claim: Modification of the triazole to an N-linked pyrrole in compound 8 resulted in a compound that no longer inhibited NADH oxidation.
source: Complete removal of the triazole group in 5 and modification of the triazole to an N-linked pyrrole in 8, also resulted in compounds that no longer inhibited NADH oxidation (Figure 2F).
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing no inhibition by compound 8.

claim: Modification of the triazole to the N-linked imidazole in compound 7 retained the inhibitory activity.
source: Most interestingly, modification of the triazole to the N-linked imidazole 7 retained the inhibitory activity.
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing similar inhibition by compound 7 compared to mubritinib.

claim: A 1,3-amidine-like motif, housed within the 1H-1,2,3-triazol-1-yl substituent, is required for complex I inhibition.
source: These data provide strong evidence that a 1,3-amidine-like motif, housed within the 1H-1,2,3-triazol-1-yl substituent, is required for complex I inhibition.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data showing that only compounds with the 1,3-nitrogen motif retain complex I inhibitory activity.

claim: The same pattern of inhibition observed for complex I was observed for ATP production in cells grown in media containing galactose.
source: The same pattern of inhibition was observed for ATP production in cells grown in media containing galactose (Figure 2G).
evidence: ATP measurement data showing correlation between complex I inhibition and ATP depletion for the compound series.

claim: Inhibition of ATP production by mubritinib results from the inhibition of complex I.
source: Therefore, inhibition of ATP production by mubritinib results from the inhibition of complex I, and depends strongly upon its 1,2,3-triazol-1-yl moiety and the embedded toxicophore.
evidence: Correlation between complex I inhibition and ATP depletion across the compound series, with both dependent on the triazole moiety.

claim: CAI has been trialled widely as an anticancer agent in single and combination therapies to treat glioblastoma, ovarian cancer and non-small cell lung cancer.
source: A structural similarity search carried out on the ChEMBL database revealed a range of terminal 1,2,3-triazole-containing drugs as putative complex I inhibitors (Supplementary file 1) including carboxyamidotriazole (9, Figure 3A), which has been trialled widely as an anticancer agent in single and combination therapies to treat glioblastoma, ovarian cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (Azad et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: The anti-proliferative and anti-metastatic properties of CAI are proposed to be mediated through the inhibition of non-voltage gated Ca2+ channels in non-excitable cells.
source: Data from a number of studies have suggested that the anti-proliferative and anti-metastatic properties of CAI (9) are mediated through the inhibition of non-voltage gated Ca2+ channels in non-excitable cells (Hupe et al., 1990), which in turn modulates downstream phosphorylation events (Bauer et al., 2000), however this has not been demonstrated directly.
evidence: Citations to previous studies proposing calcium channel inhibition mechanism.

claim: There is no significant binding of CAI to non-voltage gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Calcium binding assays performed here show clearly that there is no significant binding of CAI (9) to non-voltage gated Ca2+ channels (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Radioligand binding assay data showing no significant binding to calcium channels.

claim: CAI has been shown to affect mitochondrial calcium import and local calcium clearance.
source: It has also been shown that CAI (9) affects mitochondrial calcium import and local calcium clearance, which is essential for the maintenance of capacitative calcium entry (Mignen et al., 2005) and it was proposed that this then inhibited oxidative phosphorylation (Ju et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to published studies on CAI effects on mitochondrial calcium.

claim: CAI and compound 12 inhibited ATP production in galactose containing media much more strongly than compounds 10 and 11.
source: CAI (9) and compound 12 inhibited ATP production in galactose containing media much more strongly than compounds 10 and 11 (Figure 3B).
evidence: ATP measurement data from H9c2 cells showing differential effects of CAI variants.

claim: CAI and compound 12 decreased oxygen consumption rates much more effectively than compounds 10 and 11.
source: Similarly, CAI (9) and compound 12 decreased oxygen consumption rates much more effectively than compounds 10 and 11 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Seahorse oxygen consumption rate measurements showing differential effects of CAI variants.

claim: CAI inhibits ATP production in A549 cells grown in galactose, whereas compounds 10 and 11 have minimal effect.
source: The data show that CAI (9) inhibits ATP production in A549 cells grown in galactose, whereas 10 and 11 have minimal effect (Figure 3D) with no difference observed, as expected, in glucose containing media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: ATP measurement data from A549 lung cancer cells showing differential effects in galactose media.

claim: The basal and maximal OCR of A549 cells treated with CAI were significantly reduced, with a much smaller decrease observed with compounds 10 and 11.
source: Moreover, the basal and maximal OCR of cells treated with CAI (9) were significantly reduced, with a much smaller decrease observed with compounds 10 and 11 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Seahorse oxygen consumption rate measurements from A549 cells showing differential effects of CAI variants.

claim: Oxygen consumption was inhibited in A549 cells treated with CAI, antimycin A or piericidin following addition of pyruvate and malate.
source: In untreated cells, or cells treated with 10 and 11, there was a large increase in oxygen consumption as expected, however, oxygen consumption was inhibited in cells treated with CAI (9), antimycin A or piericidin.
evidence: Seahorse data from permeabilised A549 cells showing inhibition of complex I-driven respiration.

claim: Following addition of succinate and ADP there was an increase in OCR in CAI and piericidin-treated cells but not in cells treated with antimycin A.
source: Following addition of succinate and ADP there was an increase OCR in CAI (9) and piericidin-treated cells (but not in cells treated with antimycin A), strongly suggesting that CAI (9) is a complex I inhibitor.
evidence: Seahorse data showing restoration of respiration with succinate after CAI treatment, indicating complex I-specific inhibition.

claim: Both CAI and compound 12 inhibited complex I-driven respiration in mitochondrial membranes whereas compounds 10 and 11 have essentially no effect.
source: As expected, both CAI (9) and 12 inhibited complex I-driven respiration whereas compounds 10 and 11 have essentially no effect (Figure 3G), as reflected by the measured IC50 values for each compound (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: NADH oxidation assays in mitochondrial membranes showing differential inhibition by CAI variants.

claim: Inhibition of complex I with CAI affects signalling pathways downstream of the energy sensor AMPK, such as increased ACC phosphorylation and inhibition of mTOR signalling reducing RPS6 phosphorylation.
source: Similar to mubritinib, inhibition of complex I with CAI also affects signalling pathways downstream of the energy sensor AMPK, such as increased ACC phosphorylation and inhibition of mTOR signalling reducing RPS6 phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Western blot data showing changes in ACC and RPS6 phosphorylation following CAI treatment.

claim: ACC and RPS6 phosphorylation pathways are unaffected by the non-specific calcium channel inhibitor bepridil hydrochloride or the inactive CAI variant compound 11.
source: Importantly these pathways are unaffected by the non-specific calcium channel inhibitor bebridil hydrochloride or the inactive CAI variant compound 11.
evidence: Western blot data showing no changes in ACC and RPS6 phosphorylation with bepridil or compound 11.

claim: Treatment of the AML derived cell line HL60 with either CAI or mubritinib caused cell death in both glucose and galactose.
source: The data show that treatment of the AML derived cell line with either CAI (9) or mubritinib (1) caused cell death in both glucose and galactose, while the analogue compounds which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif had no effect (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data using DRAQ7 and Annexin-V staining showing increased cell death in HL60 cells.

claim: The analogue compounds which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif had no effect on HL60 cell death.
source: The data show that treatment of the AML derived cell line with either CAI (9) or mubritinib (1) caused cell death in both glucose and galactose, while the analogue compounds which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif had no effect (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing no increase in cell death with compounds 5 and 11.

claim: M059K, A549, U-20S, and HeLa cell lines showed no cell death in the presence of glucose.
source: The other cell lines used showed no cell death in the presence of glucose (Figure 4D and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,F and G), however again there was a correlation between the presence of the toxicophore and cell death in galactose (Figure 4C and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E and H).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing no cell death in glucose-containing media for multiple cell lines.

claim: There was a correlation between the presence of the toxicophore and cell death in galactose for M059K, A549, U-20S, and HeLa cell lines.
source: The other cell lines used showed no cell death in the presence of glucose (Figure 4D and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,F and G), however again there was a correlation between the presence of the toxicophore and cell death in galactose (Figure 4C and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E and H).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing cell death in galactose-containing media only with compounds containing the toxicophore.

claim: Both mubritinib and CAI slowed cell growth in BT474 and A549 cells grown in glucose.
source: Again, the data show a direct correlation between the presence of the 1,2,3-triazole and cell growth inhibition as both mubritinib (1) and CAI (9) slowed cell growth, whereas the analogues, which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif, had reduced or no effect.
evidence: xCELLigence real-time cell proliferation data showing reduced growth with mubritinib and CAI.

claim: The analogues which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif had reduced or no effect on cell growth in BT474 and A549 cells.
source: Again, the data show a direct correlation between the presence of the 1,2,3-triazole and cell growth inhibition as both mubritinib (1) and CAI (9) slowed cell growth, whereas the analogues, which lacked the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif, had reduced or no effect.
evidence: xCELLigence real-time cell proliferation data showing minimal effect on growth with compounds 5 and 11.

claim: Disruption of mitochondrial function selectively targets tumour cells that are dependent on oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Disruption of mitochondrial function selectively targets tumour cells that are dependent on oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle supported by the experimental findings.

claim: Due to their high energy demands, cardiac cells are disproportionately targeted by mitochondrial toxins resulting in a loss of cardiac function.
source: However, due to their high energy demands, cardiac cells are disproportionately targeted by mitochondrial toxins resulting in a loss of cardiac function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing effects on cardiomyocyte beat rate and ATP production.

claim: Mubritinib directly inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I.
source: An analysis of the effects of mubritinib on cardiac cells showed that this drug did not inhibit HER2 as reported, but directly inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing cardiac-cell beat rate, with prolonged exposure resulting in cell death.
evidence: Multiple experimental approaches including oxygen consumption measurements, NADH oxidation assays, and permeabilised cell studies.

claim: Mubritinib reduces cardiac-cell beat rate.
source: An analysis of the effects of mubritinib on cardiac cells showed that this drug did not inhibit HER2 as reported, but directly inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing cardiac-cell beat rate, with prolonged exposure resulting in cell death.
evidence: Multi-electrode array data showing decreased beat rate in hESC-cardiomyocytes.

claim: Modifying the 1H-1,2,3-triazole in mubritinib altered complex I inhibition.
source: We used a library of chemical variants of mubritinib and showed that modifying the 1H-1,2,3-triazole altered complex I inhibition, identifying the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif as the toxicophore.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data showing differential complex I inhibition across the compound series.

claim: The heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif is the toxicophore in mubritinib.
source: We used a library of chemical variants of mubritinib and showed that modifying the 1H-1,2,3-triazole altered complex I inhibition, identifying the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif as the toxicophore.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data showing that only compounds with the 1,3-nitrogen motif retain complex I inhibitory activity.

claim: The same toxicophore is present in carboxyamidotriazole (CAI).
source: The same toxicophore is present in a second anti-cancer therapeutic carboxyamidotriazole (CAI) and we demonstrate that CAI also functions through complex I inhibition, mediated by the toxicophore.
evidence: Chemical structure analysis showing the presence of the 1H-1,2,3-triazole moiety in CAI.

claim: CAI functions through complex I inhibition, mediated by the toxicophore.
source: The same toxicophore is present in a second anti-cancer therapeutic carboxyamidotriazole (CAI) and we demonstrate that CAI also functions through complex I inhibition, mediated by the toxicophore.
evidence: Multiple experimental approaches including oxygen consumption measurements, NADH oxidation assays, and structure-activity relationship studies with CAI variants.

claim: Complex I inhibition is directly linked to anti-cancer cell activity.
source: Complex I inhibition is directly linked to anti-cancer cell activity, with toxicophore modification ablating the desired effects of these compounds on cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis.
evidence: Cell death and proliferation assays showing that only compounds with the toxicophore affect cancer cell viability and growth.

claim: Toxicophore modification ablates the desired effects of mubritinib and CAI on cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis.
source: Complex I inhibition is directly linked to anti-cancer cell activity, with toxicophore modification ablating the desired effects of these compounds on cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis.
evidence: Cell death and proliferation assays showing that compounds lacking the toxicophore have no effect on cancer cell viability and growth.

claim: Mitochondrial toxicity has a major role in idiosyncratic drug toxicity.
source: It is widely accepted that disruption of mitochondrial function is a common cause of ADRs and it has been proposed that mitochondrial toxicity, which has a major role in idiosyncratic drug toxicity (Uetrecht and Naisbitt, 2013), is responsible for up to 50% of post-market drug withdrawals (Will and Dykens, 2014; Dykens and Will, 2007).
evidence: Citations to published literature on mitochondrial toxicity and drug withdrawals.

claim: Mitochondrial toxicity is responsible for up to 50% of post-market drug withdrawals.
source: It is widely accepted that disruption of mitochondrial function is a common cause of ADRs and it has been proposed that mitochondrial toxicity, which has a major role in idiosyncratic drug toxicity (Uetrecht and Naisbitt, 2013), is responsible for up to 50% of post-market drug withdrawals (Will and Dykens, 2014; Dykens and Will, 2007).
evidence: Citations to published literature on drug withdrawals.

claim: Cardiomyocytes are particularly sensitive to mitochondrial toxins that alter ATP production.
source: For example, cardiomyocytes, which have high energy requirements and are rich in mitochondria (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2016), are particularly sensitive to mitochondrial toxins that alter ATP production (Kolwicz et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to published literature and experimental data showing effects on cardiomyocyte function.

claim: Mubritinib was reported to act as a tyrosine kinase (HER2) inhibitor.
source: Given the relative paucity of mechanistic knowledge relating specific drug substructures to ADRs we carried out a detailed chemical dissection of mubritinib, which was reported to act as a tyrosine kinase (HER2) inhibitor and which has been trialled as a treatment for a range of cancers (Nagasawa et al., 2006; Ouchida et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to previous publications reporting HER2 inhibition.

claim: Mubritinib has been shown to affect energy status.
source: However, mubritinib has also been shown to affect energy status (Baccelli et al., 2019; Sridhar et al., 2003), and it was recently demonstrated to have an 'off-target' effect on mitochondrial function through inhibition of respiratory complex I in cells derived from patients with Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML), leading to a new therapeutic option (Baccelli et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to published studies showing effects on energy status.

claim: Mubritinib was recently demonstrated to have an 'off-target' effect on mitochondrial function through inhibition of respiratory complex I in cells derived from patients with AML.
source: However, mubritinib has also been shown to affect energy status (Baccelli et al., 2019; Sridhar et al., 2003), and it was recently demonstrated to have an 'off-target' effect on mitochondrial function through inhibition of respiratory complex I in cells derived from patients with Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML), leading to a new therapeutic option (Baccelli et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to Baccelli et al., 2019 study.

claim: Mubritinib's inhibitory effect on complex I negatively impacts on cardiomyocyte function.
source: Here, we show that mubritinib does not bind directly to HER2 and that its inhibitory effect on complex I negatively impacts on cardiomyocyte function, an important clinical consideration.
evidence: Experimental data showing decreased ATP production, reduced beat rate, and cell death in cardiomyocytes.

claim: CAI has been trialled as an anti-cancer agent.
source: A search of chemical space was then undertaken for the same substructure, and led to the drug carboxyamidotriazole (CAI), which has also been trialled as an anti-cancer agent (Sridhar et al., 2003; Omuro et al., 2018; Azad et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: CAI does not directly inhibit its reported target (calcium channels).
source: We show that, like mubritinib, CAI does not directly inhibit its reported target (calcium channels) and is also a potent complex I inhibitor.
evidence: Radioligand binding assay data showing no significant binding to calcium channels.

claim: CAI is a potent complex I inhibitor.
source: We show that, like mubritinib, CAI does not directly inhibit its reported target (calcium channels) and is also a potent complex I inhibitor.
evidence: NADH oxidation assays showing IC50 in the nanomolar range.

claim: Chemically altering the triazole ring moiety in CAI ablated toxicity.
source: Furthermore, like mubritinib, chemically altering the triazole ring moiety ablated toxicity.
evidence: ATP production, oxygen consumption, and cell viability data showing loss of activity with modified triazole.

claim: Mitochondrial toxicity is directly linked to anti-cancer activity for both mubritinib and CAI.
source: In both cases we show that mitochondrial toxicity is directly linked to anti-cancer activity, as chemical manipulation of the toxicophoric heterocycle ablates the desired effects of both compounds on cancer-cell proliferation and apoptosis.
evidence: Cell death and proliferation assays showing correlation between complex I inhibition and anti-cancer effects.

claim: Chemical manipulation of the toxicophoric heterocycle ablates the desired effects of both mubritinib and CAI on cancer-cell proliferation and apoptosis.
source: In both cases we show that mitochondrial toxicity is directly linked to anti-cancer activity, as chemical manipulation of the toxicophoric heterocycle ablates the desired effects of both compounds on cancer-cell proliferation and apoptosis.
evidence: Cell death and proliferation assays showing that compounds lacking the toxicophore have no effect on cancer cells.

claim: A novel toxicophoric motif has been identified that is mechanistically linked to an adverse cardiac cell event.
source: Thus, we have identified a novel toxicophoric motif that is mechanistically linked to an adverse cardiac cell event.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data linking the 1,3-nitrogen motif to complex I inhibition and cardiac toxicity.

claim: Caution must be taken when attributing a drug mechanism of action without detailed structure activity relationship (SAR) analysis.
source: Our data demonstrate that caution must be taken when attributing a drug mechanism of action without detailed structure activity relationship (SAR) analysis, since inhibition of mitochondrial function has such cell-wide effects.
evidence: Demonstration that both mubritinib and CAI were misattributed to their reported targets when they actually function through complex I inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial function has cell-wide effects.
source: Our data demonstrate that caution must be taken when attributing a drug mechanism of action without detailed structure activity relationship (SAR) analysis, since inhibition of mitochondrial function has such cell-wide effects.
evidence: Experimental data showing effects on multiple signaling pathways (AMPK, mTOR, ACC, RPS6) following complex I inhibition.

claim: Previous data have reported that mubritinib inhibits phosphorylation of HER2 in breast cancer cell lines that express high levels of this receptor.
source: Previous data have reported that mubritinib inhibits phosphorylation of HER2 in breast cancer cell lines that express high levels of this receptor (Nagasawa et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to previous publication.

claim: Mubritinib alters the phosphorylation status of proteins that sense changes in energy status and stimulate cellular proliferation, such as mTOR.
source: Furthermore, recent data have further shown that mubritinib, in common with known inhibitors of mitochondrial respiratory complex I (Sica et al., 2020), alters the phosphorylation status of proteins that sense changes in energy status and stimulate cellular proliferation, such as mTOR (Leibovitch and Topisirovic, 2018).
evidence: Citations to published studies and experimental data showing changes in mTOR signaling.

claim: Lapatinib is a specific HER2 inhibitor that blocks signalling downstream from mTOR with minimal effect on ACC phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, lapatinib, which is a specific HER2 inhibitor, blocks signalling downstream from mTOR with minimal effect on ACC phosphorylation (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ci and ii), but a large effect on RPS6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ci and ii).
evidence: Western blot data showing differential effects of lapatinib on signaling pathways compared to mubritinib.

claim: In galactose-containing media cells are predominantly reliant on mitochondria for the production of cellular ATP.
source: In galactose-containing media cells are predominantly reliant on mitochondria for the production of cellular ATP, allowing mitochondrial liabilities that are masked in glucose to be revealed (Marroquin et al., 2007; Rana et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to published methodology and experimental data showing differential effects in glucose vs galactose media.

claim: Oligomycin A, which inhibits ATP synthase, had no effect on the rotenone-sensitive OCR in the presence of FCCP.
source: As expected, oligomycin A, which inhibits ATP synthase, had no effect on the rotenone-sensitive OCR in the presence of the uncoupling agent FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone).
evidence: Seahorse oxygen consumption rate measurements showing no change in rotenone-sensitive respiration with oligomycin.

claim: Mubritinib inhibits the mitochondrial respiratory electron transport chain in cardiomyocytes.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that mubritinib (1) inhibits the mitochondrial respiratory electron transport chain in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Oxygen consumption rate data showing decreased rotenone-sensitive respiration in cardiomyocytes.

claim: All three inhibitors (mubritinib, rotenone, antimycin A) decreased the OCR in pre-treated H9c2 cells.
source: As expected, all inhibitor treatments decreased the OCR (Figure 2C).
evidence: Seahorse data from permeabilised cells showing decreased oxygen consumption with all three inhibitors.

claim: In untreated H9c2 cells, pyruvate/malate and succinate both stimulated the OCR.
source: Cells were then treated with plasma membrane permeabiliser followed by addition of ADP. Pyruvate/malate and succinate were used to drive respiration from complex I and complex II, respectively and, in untreated cells, they both stimulated the OCR.
evidence: Seahorse data showing increased oxygen consumption with substrate addition in control cells.

claim: Ketoconazole and terconazole, which contain the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif, inhibit complex I.
source: In a preliminary screen of compounds that inhibited complex I, we identified two antifungal agents, ketoconazole and terconazole, which also contained the heterocyclic 1,3-nitrogen motif embedded within a 1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl or 1H-imidazol-1-yl substituent respectively (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Screening data identifying additional compounds with the toxicophore that inhibit complex I.

claim: Rufinamide, which contains a chemically similar core scaffold to CAI, displayed no complex I inhibitory activity.
source: Interestingly, we also found that rufinamide (Supplementary file 1), which contains a chemically similar core scaffold to CAI, displayed no complex I inhibitory activity (Serreli, 2018).
evidence: Experimental data showing no inhibition of complex I by rufinamide.

claim: Rufinamide lacks an anilino nitrogen in the 5-position of the 1,2,3-triazole compared to CAI.
source: However, there are key structural differences between these two drugs and in particular, rufinamide lacks an anilino nitrogen in the 5-position of the 1,2,3-triazole, the para-chlorobenzoyl moiety and there is a chloro to fluoro switch with regards the halogen substituents on the N-benzyl group (alongside the switch in position from 3,5 to 2,6).
evidence: Chemical structure comparison between rufinamide and CAI.

claim: The logP of rufinamide (1.3) is lower than CAI (3.1), indicating a significant decrease in overall lipophilicity.
source: These observations are therefore coupled with a difference in the logP of rufinamide (1.3) when compared to CAI (3.1) which indicates a significant decrease in its overall lipophilicity and may therefore reflect a compromised pharmacokinetic-driven target engagement.
evidence: Calculated lipophilicity values for rufinamide and CAI.

claim: Neither mubritinib nor CAI directly bind their reported targets, HER2 and Ca2+ channels respectively.
source: It is of serious concern that while both mubritinib and CAI are trialled as part of anti-cancer therapies (Baccelli et al., 2019), neither directly bind their reported targets, HER2 and Ca2+ channels respectively (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Kinase assay data for mubritinib and calcium channel binding assay data for CAI showing no direct binding.

claim: Mitochondria play a central role in cell-wide processes in addition to bioenergetics and metabolism by providing a signalling hub that controls stemness, differentiation and apoptosis.
source: Mitochondria play a central role in cell-wide processes in addition to bioenergetics and metabolism by providing a signalling hub that controls stemness, differentiation and apoptosis (Guerra et al., 2017), therefore disruption of mitochondrial function can easily be misattributed to other targets, such as receptors involved in cell signalling.
evidence: Citation to published literature on mitochondrial functions.

claim: Disruption of mitochondrial function can easily be misattributed to other targets, such as receptors involved in cell signalling.
source: Mitochondria play a central role in cell-wide processes in addition to bioenergetics and metabolism by providing a signalling hub that controls stemness, differentiation and apoptosis (Guerra et al., 2017), therefore disruption of mitochondrial function can easily be misattributed to other targets, such as receptors involved in cell signalling.
evidence: Demonstration that mubritinib and CAI were misattributed to HER2 and calcium channels when they actually inhibit complex I.

claim: Both mubritinib and CAI have the potential to affect cardiac cells in situations when glucose is limiting.
source: Cardiac cells are especially sensitive to mitochondrial toxicants that alter ATP production and our data suggest that both mubritinib and CAI have the potential to affect these cell types in situations when glucose is limiting (Figures 1, 2 and 4).
evidence: Experimental data showing effects on cardiomyocyte ATP production and beat rate in galactose media.

claim: It would be important to monitor patients treated with mubritinib or CAI for changes in cardiac function during future clinical trials.
source: It would therefore be important to monitor patients treated with such agents for changes in cardiac function during future clinical trials of CAI or mubritinib.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing cardiac toxicity in cell models.

claim: Mubritinib has been used to chemo-sensitise tumour cells to other cytotoxic agents.
source: In terms of cancer treatment, mubritinib has been used to chemo-sensitise tumour cells to other cytotoxic agents.
evidence: General statement about mubritinib use in cancer treatment.

claim: In combination with AC220 (quizartinib), mubritinib reduces the viability of ovarian derived cell lines.
source: For example, in combination with AC220 (quizartinb), mubritinib reduces the viability of ovarian derived cell lines (Ouchida et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to published study on combination therapy.

claim: Sole inhibition of complex I is a viable treatment option for some cancer types.
source: However, sole inhibition of complex I is also a viable treatment option for some cancer types.
evidence: Discussion of therapeutic strategy supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: Many cancer cell subpopulations are particularly dependent upon OXPHOS for bioenergetic and biosynthetic processes.
source: Thus while drugs that target the coordinated upregulation of glycolysis that is often associated with tumorigenesis are being developed, several studies have shown that many cancer cell subpopulations are particularly dependent upon OXPHOS for bioenergetic and biosynthetic processes (Vazquez et al., 2013; Viale et al., 2014; Birsoy et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to published studies on cancer cell metabolism.

claim: Compounds that target mitochondrial complex I or ATP synthase have been shown to have efficacy in glycolysis-deficient tumour cells.
source: Compounds that target the mitochondria, either complex I including mubritinib (Baccelli et al., 2019) and IACS-010759 (Molina et al., 2018), or the ATP synthase such as Giboxin (Shi et al., 2019), have been shown to have efficacy in glycolysis–deficient tumour cells derived from patients with AML and glioblastoma (Baccelli et al., 2019; Bauer et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to published studies on mitochondrial inhibitors in cancer treatment.

claim: IACS-010759 contains a 1H-1,2,4-triazole suggesting a similar mode of action to mubritinib.
source: Interestingly, IACS-010759 (Bauer et al., 2000) contains a 1H-1,2,4-triazole suggesting a similar mode of action of this drug since this heterocycle also possesses the amidine-like nitrogen substitution pattern.
evidence: Chemical structure analysis of IACS-010759 showing presence of similar nitrogen motif.

claim: The efficacy of both mubritinib and CAI is dependent upon an amidine-like nitrogen substructure.
source: Since the efficacy of both mubritinib and CAI (Figure 4) is dependent upon an amidine-like nitrogen substructure our data suggest that new drug development programmes using this substructure within the correct chemical context could be employed to devise therapies for glycolysis deficient tumours, providing that cardiac liabilities are assessed and evaluated.
evidence: Structure-activity relationship data showing loss of efficacy when the nitrogen motif is modified.

claim: New drug development programmes using the amidine-like nitrogen substructure could be employed to devise therapies for glycolysis deficient tumours, providing that cardiac liabilities are assessed.
source: Since the efficacy of both mubritinib and CAI (Figure 4) is dependent upon an amidine-like nitrogen substructure our data suggest that new drug development programmes using this substructure within the correct chemical context could be employed to devise therapies for glycolysis deficient tumours, providing that cardiac liabilities are assessed and evaluated.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing both anti-cancer efficacy and cardiac toxicity linked to the toxicophore.

claim: Mitochondrial toxins often have a differential effect on tissue function due to organ-specific variations in the mitochondrial proteome and its function.
source: Mitochondrial toxins often have a differential effect on tissue function due to organ-specific variations in the mitochondrial proteome and its function (Johnson et al., 2007a); primarily biosynthetic and metabolic in liver, and energy production in muscle (Johnson et al., 2007b; Calvo and Mootha, 2010).
evidence: Citations to published literature on tissue-specific mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondrial function is primarily biosynthetic and metabolic in liver, and energy production in muscle.
source: Mitochondrial toxins often have a differential effect on tissue function due to organ-specific variations in the mitochondrial proteome and its function (Johnson et al., 2007a); primarily biosynthetic and metabolic in liver, and energy production in muscle (Johnson et al., 2007b; Calvo and Mootha, 2010).
evidence: Citations to published literature on tissue-specific mitochondrial function.

claim: Cardiomyocytes have high energy requirements and are rich in mitochondria.
source: For example, cardiomyocytes, which have high energy requirements and are rich in mitochondria (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2016), are particularly sensitive to mitochondrial toxins that alter ATP production (Kolwicz et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to published literature on cardiomyocyte characteristics.

claim: Mitochondrial toxicity affects bioenergetics, metabolism, signalling and oxidative stress.
source: Mitochondria are central to many cell-wide processes so mitochondrial toxicity affects bioenergetics, metabolism, signalling and oxidative stress (Meyer et al., 2018) in addition to impacting stemness, differentiation and apoptosis (Guerra et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to published literature on mitochondrial functions.

claim: Off-target drug toxicity resulting in impairment of mitochondrial function can easily be misattributed to other targets and cellular processes.
source: Due to these pleiotropic roles, 'off-target' drug toxicity resulting in impairment of mitochondrial function can easily be misattributed to other targets and cellular processes.
evidence: General statement supported by the demonstration that mubritinib and CAI were misattributed to other targets.
